params.title: Other Equipment and Networks
params.subtitle: Computers, Ethernet, the NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000 ship networks, and the bridge instruments that use them.

onScreen: Computers, Ethernet, NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000, and bridge instruments
scenes.narration: A GMDSS maintainer, the technician who keeps a ship's Global Maritime Distress and Safety System working, looks after more than radios. The same person gets called when the office computer won't start or the bridge network drops out. This lesson covers that other equipment. First, computers and the networks that link them. Then NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000, named after the National Marine Electronics Association: the 2 networks that let a ship's instruments share data. After that, the instruments themselves, from depth finders and compasses to the auto pilot and the data recorder. By the end you'll be able to troubleshoot common computer faults, explain how ship networks are wired, and recall the numbers the exam asks about.

params.title: Inside a computer: follow the path

blocks.label: Operating system
blocks.note: The main program, such as Windows

onScreen: Printer path: operating system, printer queue, printer
Picture path: video card, 15 pin video connector, monitor
scenes.narration: First, the computer, because troubleshooting one is mostly a matter of following a path. The processor is the chip that does the work. The memory, called RAM for random access memory, holds what it's working on, and the hard drive keeps files even with the power off. The operating system, such as Windows, is the main program that runs everything. A printout follows one path: through the operating system's printer queue, the waiting line of print jobs, and out to the printer. The picture follows another: the video card, also called the graphics card, makes the picture signal and sends it through a 15 pin video connector to the monitor. When something fails, first ask which path it's on.

params.title: The printer won't print
items: Frozen printer queue: jobs stuck in the waiting line
Out of toner or ink
A paper jam
Not a likely reason: a defective graphics card

onScreen: Not a likely reason: a defective graphics card
scenes.narration: So the printer won't print a document. Walk along the printer path. The printer queue may be frozen: one stuck job blocks the line, so nothing behind it moves. The printer may be out of toner or ink, the powder or liquid that makes the marks. Or there may be a paper jam. Each of those is a likely reason. Now, which is not a likely reason? A defective graphics card. The graphics card only drives the monitor; it isn't on the printer path at all. The exam asks for the reason that is not likely, so the graphics card is the one to pick.

params.title: No display on the monitor
items: Bad video card
Bad 15 pin video connector
No power to the monitor
Not the cause: a CD-ROM drive or a fragmented hard drive

onScreen: Not a CD-ROM drive or a fragmented hard drive
scenes.narration: Now the other path: no display on the monitor. The most likely causes sit along the picture path: a bad video card, a bad 15 pin video connector, or no power to the monitor. Check the easy one first: is the monitor plugged in and on? A CD-ROM drive, for compact disc read-only memory, just reads discs; it has nothing to do with the picture. Neither does a fragmented hard drive, where files are stored in scattered pieces; that slows a computer but never blanks the screen. So the keyed answer stays on the picture path: bad video card, bad 15 pin video connector, or no power to the monitor. The trap choice slips in a bad CD-ROM.

params.title: Switching on: the BIOS takes charge
items: The operating system is stored on a drive: something must start it
BIOS: the basic input-output system
A small program in a chip on the main circuit board
Like a caretaker: checks the building, then opens up

onScreen: Something must start the operating system
A program in a chip on the main board
Checks first, then starts things up
scenes.narration: Both of those faults happen on a computer that's already running. But what happens before that, when you switch it on? The operating system is stored on a drive, and something has to start it. That job belongs to the BIOS, the basic input-output system. It's a small program built into a chip on the computer's main circuit board, so it's ready the instant the power comes on. Think of a caretaker who arrives first, checks the building, then unlocks the doors for the staff. The BIOS works the same way: it checks the computer, then starts the operating system.

params.title: Start-up: P.O.S.T., then the bootstrap loader

blocks.label: Bootstrap loader
blocks.note: Finds and starts the operating system

onScreen: Bootstrap loader: finds and starts the operating system
scenes.narration: Here are those 2 steps in order. When the power comes on, the BIOS first runs P.O.S.T., the power-on self-test: a quick check that the memory, keyboard, video and drives answer. If something fails, the computer beeps or shows an error. Then comes the bootstrap loader, which finds the operating system on a drive and starts it. The name comes from the old saying about pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps, since the computer is starting itself. Starting up this way is called booting.

params.title: The BIOS: 4 main functions
items: P.O.S.T. and the bootstrap loader: the first 2
BIOS drivers: basic control of keyboard, screen and drives
BIOS setup: the settings screen, such as boot order

scenes.narration: Those are 2 of the BIOS's 4 main functions. The third is the BIOS drivers. A driver is software that lets a computer control a piece of equipment, and the BIOS drivers give basic control of the keyboard, screen and drives until the operating system takes over. The fourth is BIOS setup: a settings screen you open by pressing a key during start-up. It stores choices such as which drive to boot from. So the 4 main functions of the BIOS are P.O.S.T., the bootstrap loader, BIOS drivers and BIOS setup.

params.title: BIOS function or not?
rows: No: loaded by the operating system

onScreen: P.O.S.T., bootstrap loader, BIOS drivers, BIOS setup: yes
Printer drivers: loaded by the operating system
CPU setup, RAM setup, disc partitions: no
scenes.narration: The exam's wrong answers swap one of those 4 for something else. Printer drivers are the favorite swap. But a printer isn't needed to start the computer, so the operating system loads the printer driver later, once it's running. That makes it an operating system job, not a BIOS function. Other wrong lists name CPU setup and RAM setup, CPU meaning central processing unit, another name for the processor. Some name disc partitions, the sections a drive is divided into. None of those is among the 4 main functions.

params.title: Power on, but it won't boot
items: Power is on, but the operating system won't load
The loader searches the drives in the boot device order
Wrong order, or drive not detected: nothing to start
Fix: use BIOS setup mode to check the BIOS settings

onScreen: Power on, operating system won't load
Loader searches in boot device order
Wrong order or drive not detected
Fix: check the settings in BIOS setup mode
scenes.narration: BIOS setup is also where you go when the power is on but the computer won't boot into the operating system. The fans spin, but instead of Windows you get a message that no boot device was found. Why? The bootstrap loader searches the drives in the order the BIOS settings list them. If that boot device order is wrong, or the BIOS hasn't detected the drive, the loader finds nothing to start. So use the BIOS setup mode to check for proper BIOS settings, such as boot device order and drive detection. Checking the CPU fan, cleaning a plug-in card's contacts, or unplugging the external cables won't fix a wrong setting.

params.title: Windows XP: which disc drives are fitted?

blocks.label: System Information
blocks.note: In System Tools: lists each drive type

onScreen: System Information: shows the disc drive types
scenes.narration: Once the computer does boot, you may need to know what drives it has, say before replacing one. Windows XP is an older version of Microsoft Windows, still found on some ship equipment. To determine the type of disc drives in a Windows XP system, click Start, then Programs, then Accessories, and then System Information. On the real menu, System Information sits one folder further in, under System Tools. It lists the computer's hardware, including the type of each drive. The trap choices send you to a System Information button straight off the Start menu, or into the Control Panel's sound or taskbar settings; those won't show you the drives.

params.title: Replacing a CD-ROM drive
rows: Yes: same as the old drive
No: a faster drive is fine

onScreen: Interface system: must match the old drive
Data transfer rate: need not match
RAM: not part of the drive
scenes.narration: Say System Information shows a CD-ROM drive that has failed, and you're replacing it. The key word is interface: the type of connection between the drive and the computer, meaning both the plug and the signals it carries. Common interface systems go by their initials: IDE/ATAPI, SATA and SCSI. IDE/ATAPI uses a wide flat ribbon cable; SATA uses a thin one. Like a plug and socket, the interface has to fit, so the replacement drive should use the same interface system as the old drive. Otherwise it won't connect. Its speed and data transfer rate need not match; a faster drive works fine. RAM, the computer's working memory, isn't part of a CD-ROM drive, so there's no RAM to match.

params.title: From one computer to a network
items: Network: computers linked so they can share data
Node: any device on the network, such as a computer or printer
LAN: a local area network, inside one ship or building
Ethernet: the usual way to wire a LAN

scenes.narration: That covers single computers. But aboard ship, computers rarely work alone. The office computer sends to a shared printer, and the bridge computers share charts and email. Linking them makes a network: computers connected so they can share data. Each device on the network, a computer or a printer, is called a node. A network inside one ship or building is a LAN, a local area network. And the usual way to wire a LAN is Ethernet. Data travels on it in short bundles called packets, rather like envelopes, each carrying the address of the node it's for.

params.title: Ethernet: a star around the central hub

blocks.label: Central hub
blocks.note: Passes each packet to the other nodes

onScreen: Each node: a home run cable back to the central hub
scenes.narration: So how are Ethernet nodes wired together? They're interconnected in a star, with a box called a hub at the center. Each node has its own cable running straight back to the central hub, like a spoke of a wheel. That cable is called a home run, because it runs all the way home to the hub without joining any other cable. The hub passes each packet it receives on to the other nodes. Modern networks often use a switch, a smarter kind of hub, in its place, but the star is the same. On the exam, the home run goes back to the central hub; router, backbone and computer are the trap answers.

params.title: One at a time: the collision domain
items: The hub passes every packet to every node
2 nodes sending at once: a collision
Collision domain: the nodes that can collide with each other
Only 1 can transmit at a time, so they share the bandwidth

onScreen: Bandwidth shared: 1 transmits at a time
scenes.narration: Because a hub passes everything to everyone, there's a catch. If 2 nodes send at once, their signals collide and both are garbled, so each waits a random moment and tries again. All the nodes that can collide this way form a collision domain. Within the same collision domain, only 1 node can transmit at a time, so the available bandwidth, the network's capacity to carry data, is shared between all the nodes. It's like a single-lane bridge: everyone gets across, but one at a time, so more traffic means slower trips. On the exam, bandwidth is shared within the same collision domain, not the same compartment, address range or star topology, topology meaning the shape of the wiring.

params.title: Reading the name: 10Base-T
items: Bit: a single 1 or 0
10 or 100: the speed, in megabits per second
Base: the cable carries just this one signal
T: twisted pair, 2 wires twisted around each other

onScreen: Base: one signal on the cable
scenes.narration: That's the shape of the network. Now the cable that makes each home run. You'll see Ethernet types named like 10Base-T and 100Base-TX, and each part of the name means something. Data is counted in bits: a bit is a single 1 or 0. The first number is the speed: 10 or 100 megabits, that's millions of bits, per second. Base means the cable carries just this one signal. And the T stands for twisted pair: 2 wires twisted around each other. Twisting makes interference, electrical noise picked up from nearby equipment, hit both wires equally, and the receiver, which looks at the difference between them, cancels it out.

So which cable do these systems use? 10Base-T and 100Base-TX systems generally use CAT-5 cable, short for category 5, with 4 twisted pairs: 8 wires in all. The trap answer offers CAT-5 with 2 twisted pairs, but standard CAT-5 always has 4 pairs inside. Coax, a single wire inside a round shield, belongs to older Ethernet types, and fiber optic, which carries light instead of electricity, to others. So the answer to remember is CAT-5 with 4 twisted pairs.

params.title: USB 2.0 cables: 5 meters max
items: USB: Universal Serial Bus, for keyboards, printers and memory sticks
Peripheral: a device plugged into the computer
USB 2.0 cable: 5 meters max, hub to hub or hub to peripheral
More distance? Add a hub: another 5 meters

onScreen: Add a hub for more distance
scenes.narration: One more cable on the exam isn't Ethernet: USB, the Universal Serial Bus, the everyday plug for keyboards, printers and memory sticks. A device plugged into a computer this way is a peripheral, and a USB hub is a small box that turns one USB socket into several. The maximum length of a USB 2.0 cable between 2 hubs, or between a hub and a peripheral, is 5 meters. Why so short? The computer expects each reply within a tiny window of time, and a longer cable delays and weakens the signal. To cover more distance, add a hub; each new cable is again limited to 5 meters. On the exam, don't be tempted by 10, 15 or 20 meters.

params.title: Routers and IP addresses
items: Router: links the ship's network to another network
IP address: each device's number on the network
Written as 4 numbers separated by dots
The router has its own address, set at the factory

scenes.narration: So much for the cables inside the ship. To reach beyond the ship's own network, say to the internet over the satellite link, you need a router: a box that connects one network to another and sends each packet the right way. For that, every device needs an address. Its IP address, IP standing for Internet Protocol, is the device's number on the network, rather like a house number on a street. It's written as 4 numbers separated by dots. The router has an IP address of its own, set at the factory, and you'll need it to set the router up.

params.title: Router addresses, for the exam
items: Router defaults often start with 192.168: a block for local networks
In practice: 192.168.2.0 names a whole network
The usual default there is 192.168.2.1

scenes.narration: Which addresses do routers come with? Many use addresses starting with 192.168, a block set aside for local networks. For the exam, the most commonly used router IP addresses are 192.168.1.1, 192.168.0.1 and 192.168.2.0. In practice, 192.168.2.0 is normally a network address, the name of a whole network rather than of one device, and the usual default is 192.168.2.1. But on the exam, choose that set anyway: it's the only one where every address starts with 192.168.

params.title: Installing a router: the first steps

onScreen: Enter the router's address for network admin
scenes.narration: Once you know that address, setting up is simple, because a router has its own built-in settings page. With a computer connected to the router, the initial steps are: open a web browser, enter the router's address for network admin, meaning the settings that manage the network, and then enter the username and password. The browser talks to the router directly, so no internet access and no download are needed, and no setup software either. Nor do you type in the addresses of all the stations on the network; the exam offers those steps as wrong choices.

onScreen: Chart display, radar and DSC radio: listeners
NMEA sentences: short lines of text
scenes.narration: That's the office side. Now the bridge, where the instruments share their readings. The GPS receiver works out the ship's position from Global Positioning System satellites. Other units need that position: the chart display; the radar, which shows nearby ships and land; and the DSC radio, the digital selective calling radio that sends distress alerts. The rules for sharing it come from the National Marine Electronics Association, or NMEA. The unit that sends is the talker; the units that receive are listeners. The data travels as sentences: short lines of text, like telegrams, saying who is talking, what kind of data it is, and the values. There are 2 NMEA standards: NMEA 0183, the older one, and NMEA 2000.

params.title: NMEA 0183: serial data
labels: Serial: 1 bit at a time, one after another
Parallel: several bits side by side, on several wires
NMEA 0183 is serial: not parallel, CAN bus or Ethernet

scenes.narration: First, NMEA 0183. It uses serial data communication, the same serial as in Universal Serial Bus. Serial means the bits go down one pair of wires 1 at a time, one after another, like people in single file through a door. On screen, the line steps between high and low, and each level stands for a 1 or a 0. The other way is parallel: several wires side by side, each carrying a bit at once, like a crowd through a wide gate. NMEA 0183 sends its sentences serially, usually at 4800 bits per second. On the exam, NMEA 0183 is serial: not parallel, not Ethernet, and not a CAN bus, a Controller Area Network, which comes with NMEA 2000.

params.title: NMEA 0183: the RS422 standard
rows: Early NMEA 0183 and old computer serial ports

scenes.narration: Which electrical standard carries those bits? The current and most recent version of NMEA 0183 uses the RS422 standard for data communications. RS stands for recommended standard. RS422 is balanced: the talker sends each bit on a pair of wires as mirror images, one wire high while the other is low, and the listener reads the difference. Noise that hits both wires equally cancels out, the same trick as twisted pair. Only 1 talker is allowed per line, though it can feed several listeners: 2 talkers on the same pair would fight each other. Early versions of NMEA 0183 were compatible with RS232, the old computer serial port standard. RS232, RS485 and ISO 11783 are the trap answers.

callouts.label: Trace: an NMEA 0183 signal swings above and below 0 volts
A unit must survive ±15 volts without damage
Older RS232 style talkers can swing up to 15 volts either way

onScreen: Signal swings above and below 0 volts
RS232 style talkers swing up to 15 volts
scenes.narration: RS232 matters for one more NMEA 0183 number, a voltage limit. Voltage is the electrical push behind a signal, like water pressure in a pipe. An oscilloscope, an instrument that draws a signal's voltage over time, shows an NMEA 0183 signal swinging above and below 0 volts. An NMEA 0183 unit must be capable of handling a maximum signal voltage range of plus or minus 15 volts without damage. Why that much? A listener may end up wired to an older RS232 style talker, whose signals can swing up to 15 volts either way. Normal NMEA 0183 signals swing less, but the input must survive the worst case. Plus or minus 5, 10 and 12 volts are the trap answers.

params.title: The problem: ground loops
items: Ground: each unit's 0 volt reference, tied to its metal chassis
Grounds in different places sit at slightly different voltages
Shield grounded at both ends: current flows round a ground loop
Result: noise and data errors

onScreen: Both ends grounded: a ground loop
scenes.narration: Voltage also lies behind a wiring problem NMEA 0183 must avoid. Every unit has a ground: its 0 volt point, the level its other voltages are measured from, tied to its metal case, the chassis. Grounds in different parts of a ship can sit at slightly different voltages. The data cable has a shield, a foil or braid wrapped around the wires that catches interference and drains it to ground. If that shield is grounded at both ends, it joins the 2 grounds, and current, the flow of electricity, runs along it, like water through a pipe between 2 tanks at slightly different heights. That path is a ground loop, and its current adds noise and data errors.

params.title: The fix: opto-isolators, one grounded end

blocks.label: Talker
blocks.note: Shield grounded to this chassis only

onScreen: Shield grounded to the talker chassis only
scenes.narration: NMEA 0183 breaks the loop in 2 ways. First, opto-isolators must be used. An opto-isolator is a tiny light and a light sensor sealed together. The incoming signal flashes the light, and the sensor facing it switches in step. The data crosses the gap as light, so no wire joins the talker's ground to the listener's. Second, the cable shield should be grounded to the talker chassis only. With 1 grounded end there's no loop, and the shield still drains away interference. So the keyed statement is: opto-isolators must be used, and the shield is grounded to the talker chassis only. Grounding both ends, or the listener end only, is wrong, and version 2 devices don't use higher voltages.

params.title: Watching NMEA 0183 data on a PC
items: Sentences are plain text, so a PC can show them
Connect the NMEA 0183 line to a PC serial port
HyperTerminal shows each sentence as it arrives
Logging: saving the sentences to a file
Not Excel, Windows Explorer or Microsoft Word

onScreen: Plain text: a PC can show it
NMEA 0183 line to a PC serial port
scenes.narration: Even with good wiring, an instrument sometimes isn't getting its data. Then you want to see what the talker is actually sending. Because NMEA 0183 sentences are plain text, a PC, a personal computer, can show them. Connect the line to the PC's serial port and run a terminal program, which simply displays whatever text arrives. A typical PC program used widely for logging and troubleshooting NMEA 0183 data is HyperTerminal, which came with older versions of Windows. Logging means saving the sentences to a file to study later. Excel, Windows Explorer and Microsoft Word can't open a serial port, so they're the wrong choices.

onScreen: A line per talker versus a shared backbone
scenes.narration: That's NMEA 0183. Its single talker per line becomes a problem on a busy bridge. Every talker needs its own line, and feeding several talkers to one listener needs an extra box, a multiplexer, to merge them. NMEA 2000 solves this. It's a true network: one shared cable, called the backbone, runs through the ship, and every device plugs into it and can both talk and listen. So an important difference between NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000 is single talker versus multi-talkers. NMEA 2000 is built on a CAN bus, a Controller Area Network: a system first designed for cars, so that many controllers could share one pair of data wires, taking turns.

blocks.label: Tee
blocks.note: A T-shaped joint in the backbone

onScreen: A drop cable from each tee to one device
scenes.narration: So what does that backbone look like? The backbone cable is the main trunk, running the length of the network. Wherever a device joins it, there's a tee, a T-shaped connector. A power cable joins at a tee too, feeding power onto the backbone, because NMEA 2000 carries power for its devices in the same cable as the data. From each tee, a short drop cable runs to one device, such as a GPS receiver or a display. Every device talks and listens on that one shared backbone.

params.title: NMEA 2000 part or not?
rows: Backbone cables, tees, drops, power cables

onScreen: Backbone cables, tees, drop cables, power cables
scenes.narration: One part is still missing. At each end of the backbone sits a terminating resistor. A resistor is a part that resists current. Here it soaks up the signal when it reaches the end of the line, so it doesn't bounce back like a wave off a harbor wall and garble the next message. So NMEA 2000 networks are built from backbone cables, tees, drop cables, power cables and terminating resistors. Multiplexers and combiners are NMEA 0183 boxes that merge talkers, which a shared backbone doesn't need. Routers belong to computer networks. When the exam asks which list is not NMEA 2000 components, pick multiplexers, combiners and routers.

params.title: Drop cables: 6 meters max
items: Drop cable: from a tee to 1 device
Maximum length to a single device: 6 meters
Not 12, 18 or 24 meters

scenes.narration: Back to those drop cables: they have a limit. The maximum length for a drop cable to a single NMEA 2000 device is 6 meters. Why? A drop is a dead-end side branch off the backbone. Signals reflect back from the end of a long branch, the same kind of bounce the terminating resistors stop at the ends of the backbone, and disturb the messages. A long drop also loses voltage on the way to the device. So keep each drop to 6 meters or less. 12, 18 and 24 meters are the wrong choices.

callouts.label: Reading must stay within 9 to 16 volts
Probes across the backbone's power supply pair

onScreen: Probes across the power supply pair
scenes.narration: Then there's the power cable. It feeds the backbone's power supply pair: 2 wires that carry DC, direct current, the steady one-way current a battery gives, usually from the ship's 12 volt supply. The voltage of the NMEA 2000 backbone power supply pair must be maintained within 9 to 16 volts. The danger is voltage drop: just as water pressure falls along a long hose, the voltage sags along a long, busy backbone, and it must not fall below 9 volts at any device. To check, set a multimeter, a handheld test meter, to DC volts and put its probes across the pair. 0 to 5, 10.5 to 13.6, and 12 to 24 volts are the trap ranges.

Every device on the backbone draws some current from that power pair. Current is measured in amps, and a milliamp is a thousandth of an amp. NMEA 2000 certified devices state their current requirements in LENs, Load Equivalency Numbers. 1 LEN is equal to 50 milliamps. Say a device is rated 3 LEN. How much current can it draw? Each LEN stands for 50 milliamps, so multiply: 3 times 50 milliamps is 150 milliamps. That's a small current, which makes sense for an instrument. Adding up the LENs of every device tells you whether the power supply and cable can carry the load. 1 amp, 500 milliamps and 25 milliamps are the trap answers.

params.title: Backbone speed: 250, for the exam
items: Data rate: how many bits are sent each second
For the exam: 250 bps
In reality: 250 kilobits per second

scenes.narration: That's the power side. Now the data: how fast does the backbone carry it? Speed here means the data rate: how many bits are sent each second. On a CAN bus, every device shares the same pair of wires and must read every other device's bits, so they all signal at the same fixed rate, set by the standard. For the exam, the NMEA 2000 backbone operating speed is keyed as 250 bits per second. The real backbone runs at 250 kilobits per second, that's 250 thousand bits each second. But the exam choices are all plain bits per second, so choose 250, not 500, 1500 or 2000.

Last NMEA 2000 fact: seeing the data. NMEA 0183 sentences could go straight into a PC running HyperTerminal. NMEA 2000 can't, because it's a CAN bus: its messages are packed in a format a PC's serial port doesn't understand. So viewing NMEA 2000 data requires a gateway. A gateway is a translator box. It reads the NMEA 2000 messages and passes them on in a format the viewing equipment understands, such as USB, Ethernet or NMEA 0183. On the exam, the answer is gateway. A voltmeter only measures voltage, not messages. Converter sounds close, but it isn't the keyed word, and HyperTerminal alone can't read a CAN bus.

blocks.label: Transducer
blocks.note: Under the hull: turns it into sound

scenes.narration: With the networks done, let's meet the instruments they connect, starting with the depth finder, also called an echo sounder. It works like shouting at a cliff and timing the echo. A transmitter makes a short electrical burst. A transducer under the hull, a device that turns electrical signals into sound and back, sends it straight down as a pulse of sound. The sound bounces off the seabed and comes back up to the transducer. Sound travels through seawater at about 1500 meters per second. Multiply the echo's travel time by that speed, then halve the result, since the sound went down and back up: that's the depth.

What kind of sound does it use? Frequency is how many times each second the sound vibrates, measured in hertz, and a kilohertz is a thousand vibrations a second. Human hearing tops out around 20 kilohertz, so the trap range of 200 to 800 hertz is ordinary audible sound, far too low. Depth finding equipment commonly uses frequencies of 200 to 400 kilohertz: ultrasound, far above hearing. Why there? Higher frequencies make a narrower beam and finer detail, but seawater absorbs them faster. That rules out 1000 to 2600 and 4,000 to 6,000 kilohertz: they would be absorbed too quickly. 200 to 400 kilohertz is the balance: fine detail, and still a useful depth.

params.title: Depth finder pulse widths
labels: Pulse width: how long each burst lasts
Short pulses: fine resolution in shallow water

onScreen: Pulse width: how long each burst lasts
scenes.narration: The depth finder doesn't send that sound nonstop. It goes out in pulses: short bursts, with silence in between to listen for the echo. Pulse width is how long each burst lasts. A microsecond is a millionth of a second. Depth finding equipment commonly uses pulse widths of 25 to 600 microseconds. Short pulses give fine resolution in shallow water: close echoes stay separate instead of blurring together. Longer pulses put more energy into the water, for deeper soundings: the echo still comes back strong from far below. 10 to 30 microseconds leaves out the longer pulses deep water needs. And 2 to 20 or 50 to 200 milliseconds, thousandths of a second, would be far too long.

params.title: What a gyro compass does
rows: Pulled off by the ship's steel?

onScreen: Not pulled off by the ship's steel
scenes.narration: The depth finder tells you what's under the ship. The next instrument tells you which way it's pointing: the gyro compass. A compass gives the ship's heading, the direction its bow is pointing. A magnetic compass points to magnetic north, and the ship's own steel can pull it off. A gyro compass finds true north, the direction of the earth's North Pole, by sensing the earth's rotation instead of its magnetism. Older gyro compasses do this with a heavy wheel, the rotor, spinning very fast; once it settles, its spin axis lines up with north. The gyro's heading feeds the radar, the auto pilot and the chart display, so a gyro fault shows up all over the bridge.

params.title: Older gyro compass: the carbon pile
items: Carbon pile: a stack of carbon disks
Squeeze harder: lower resistance; ease off: higher resistance
So it acts as a variable resistor, set by the output voltage
Purpose: voltage regulation

onScreen: Carbon pile: a stack of carbon disks
scenes.narration: Those older spinning gyros needed a steady electrical supply, often from a motor-generator, an electric motor turning a generator. That's where the carbon pile comes in. A carbon pile is a stack of carbon disks. Resistance is how strongly something opposes current, like a narrow section of pipe. Squeeze the stack harder and its resistance drops; ease off and it rises. That makes the pile a variable resistor. The output voltage sets the squeeze: if the voltage creeps up, the pile loosens, its resistance rises, and the voltage comes back down. So the carbon pile on an older gyro compass provides voltage regulation. Ballast regulation, precession control and pendulum effect errors are mechanical gyro terms, and the trap answers.

Newer ships often use a different design: the fiber-optic gyro compass. A fiber-optic coil is a long strand of glass fiber wound into a coil, with light sent both ways around it. If the coil turns, one beam has farther to go than the other, and the difference shows how fast it's turning. 3 coils, one for each direction of turn, measure the earth's rotation. A dual-axis electronic level sensor checks level in 2 directions. From those, the computer works out true north. So the fiber-optic gyro compass uses 3 fiber-optic coils and a dual-axis electronic level sensor, with no spinning rotor at all. Choices with fewer coils, accelerometers or a yaw detector are wrong.

params.title: SSAS: a silent alarm
items: Ship Security Alert System: for piracy or hijacking
Hidden buttons: one on the bridge, at least one elsewhere
Covert: the alert is secret
No alarm sounds aboard

scenes.narration: Not every danger at sea comes from the weather or the seabed, so from navigation we turn to security. The Ship Security Alert System, or SSAS, is for piracy or a hijacking. Hidden buttons, one on the bridge and at least one elsewhere aboard, send a covert, meaning secret, alert. No alarm sounds aboard, so the attackers aren't tipped off that help has been called. A crew member can press a button and carry on as if nothing has happened.

onScreen: No all ships alert on VHF-DSC or MF-HF
scenes.narration: So where does that secret alert go? SSAS operates by sending the alert through the Inmarsat-C terminal, the ship's satellite text message terminal, to specific addresses set up in advance, such as the shipping company's security officer. It does not send an all ships alert on VHF-DSC, the very high frequency DSC radio, or on MF-HF, the medium and high frequency bands. An all ships alert would be heard by every radio nearby, including the attackers'. And the keyed answer says specific addresses, not the rescue coordination center.

params.title: AIS: every ship announces itself
labels: Each ship's AIS broadcasts its identity, position, course and speed

onScreen: Each AIS broadcasts identity, position, course and speed
scenes.narration: SSAS keeps quiet on purpose. AIS, the Automatic Identification System, does the opposite: it announces the ship to everyone. Every ship's AIS unit automatically broadcasts the ship's identity, position, course and speed by radio, over and over, and listens for everyone else's. Picture each ship calling out: this is my name, here I am, this is where I'm heading. Nobody has to press anything; that's what automatic means. On the radar, each nearby ship shows as an echo, the bright spot its radar reflection makes, and the AIS reports put a name and course beside it. So you know not just that a ship is there, but which ship it is and where it's going.

Those reports go out by VHF radio, the same very high frequency band as the ship's voice radio. A channel is a numbered frequency slot, and megahertz means millions of cycles each second. AIS units use 2 VHF channels: channel 87B at 161.975 megahertz, and channel 88B at 162.025 megahertz. Each unit alternates between the 2, so interference on one channel doesn't silence a ship. Watch the trap choices: 65B and 66B, or 18B and 19B, are other marine channels, and 16 and 70 are kept for voice distress calling and DSC. The pair to know is 87B at 161.975, and 88B at 162.025 megahertz.

params.title: AIS data: 9.6 kbs GMSK
labels: Data rate: 9.6 kbs, kilobits per second
Shift keying: the frequency shifts for each 1 or 0
Smoothed shifts keep the signal inside its channel

onScreen: Smoothed to stay in its channel
scenes.narration: How does AIS put its data on the radio wave? That's called modulation. AIS units send 9.6 kilobits per second using GMSK modulation: Gaussian minimum shift keying. Shift keying means the transmitter shifts its frequency slightly up or down for each 1 or 0, which is why the wave on screen bunches up and spreads out. Minimum shift means using the smallest shift that still works, which keeps the signal narrow. Gaussian refers to a smoothing filter, named after the mathematician Gauss, that rounds off each change so the signal stays inside its channel. The trap choices use the wrong channels or 4.8 kilobits per second. So: 87B and 88B, 9.6 kilobits per second, GMSK.

params.title: Electronic charts and ECDIS
items: Electronic chart system: the nautical chart on a screen
The ship's own position drawn on it live
ECDIS: the approved kind, which can replace paper charts

onScreen: Electronic chart system: the chart on a screen
scenes.narration: Now the last key topic: the bridge systems that bring all these readings together. First, the chart display you met as a listener on the NMEA network. It's called an electronic chart system. It shows the nautical chart, the seafarer's map of coasts, depths and hazards, on a screen, with the ship's own position drawn on it live. The approved kind, which can stand in for paper charts, is ECDIS, the Electronic Chart Display and Information System. To draw the ship on the chart, the system needs data from other instruments.

onScreen: SSAS is not a chart input
scenes.narration: Which ones? Electronic chart system data inputs include position from the GPS, speed from the speed log, an instrument that measures the ship's speed, depth from the depth finder, and radar, whose picture can be laid over the chart. SSAS is not a chart input: it's the covert security alert, and it supplies no chart data. So on the exam, the list radar, SSAS and position is the incorrect one.

params.title: C-Map charts: a license for each computer
items: C-Map: a commercial brand of electronic charts
Enter the license information for each computer being used
Not just once in a master terminal

scenes.narration: Before the charts appear, they have to be licensed. C-Map is a commercial brand of electronic charts, and its licenses are tied to the specific computer they're entered on. So before using C-Map charts for an electronic chart system, license information must be entered for each computer being used. Entering it once in a master terminal doesn't unlock the charts on the others. Downloading the charts from the internet, or plugging a dongle, a small security key, into the master terminal, isn't the procedure the exam wants either. Each computer needs its own license information.

params.title: What an auto pilot does
items: Auto pilot: steers the ship on a set course
Course information: the set course and the gyro heading
Steering gear: the machinery that moves the rudder

onScreen: Auto pilot: steers a set course
scenes.narration: The chart shows where the ship should go. The auto pilot keeps it on that course, steering automatically. Think about how a helmsman steers. They look at the compass, compare the heading with the course they've been given, and turn the wheel to correct the difference. The auto pilot does the same. Its course information is the set course compared with the actual heading from the gyro compass. When they differ, it orders the steering gear, the powerful machinery that moves the rudder, to swing the rudder over. But how does it know how far the rudder has actually moved?

onScreen: Rudder feedback unit: necessary, reports the rudder angle
Auto pilot drives the steering gear
scenes.narration: That's the job of the rudder feedback unit, a sensor at the rudder that reports the actual rudder angle back to the auto pilot. The auto pilot compares the angle it ordered with the angle reported, and stops the steering gear at the right point. Without that feedback it would be steering blind. Order, move, report, correct: that's a loop. So the rudder feedback unit is a necessary component of an auto pilot, and the inputs normally required are course information and rudder feedback. GPS can be a useful extra input, but it isn't necessary. Yaw sensors, which sense the bow swinging side to side, aren't required either. Nor are radar data, engine RPM, meaning revolutions per minute, or SSAS.

params.title: What the Vessel Data Recorder records

onScreen: Audio from the bridge and VHF radio
scenes.narration: One more system, and it keeps a record of all the others: the Vessel Data Recorder, or VDR, also called the voyage data recorder. It's the ship's black box, like an airliner's flight recorder. It runs all the time, so after an accident investigators can replay what happened on the bridge. It records items such as the date, time and position, the speed and heading, the depth of water, the radar picture, audio from the bridge microphones, and VHF radio communications. Rudder feedback may be an input too. Notice that most of the instruments in this lesson feed it.

params.title: Not VDR inputs: EGC data and MSI
items: EGC: Enhanced Group Call, Inmarsat-C broadcasts to groups of ships
MSI: Maritime Safety Information, navigation and weather warnings
Neither is a VDR input
On the exam: the list with EGC data or MSI is the wrong one

onScreen: The list with EGC or MSI is wrong
scenes.narration: Now the 2 items that are not VDR inputs. EGC, Enhanced Group Call, is the Inmarsat-C service that broadcasts safety messages to groups of ships at once. MSI, Maritime Safety Information, means the navigation warnings, weather warnings and forecasts broadcast to ships. Both arrive as messages on their own receivers, and neither is among the items the VDR records. So on the exam, the list heading, depth of water, EGC data and radar is the inaccurate one. And the statement that data input may include MSI is the one that's not true.

params.title: How long the VDR keeps its data

badges.label: Data Acquisition Unit (DAU)
badges.note: May have data storage this long

onScreen: Crash Survivable Module: up to 12 hours
Data Acquisition Unit: as long as 30 days
scenes.narration: So where does all that recorded data go? The VDR has 2 storage parts to know. The Crash Survivable Module, or CSM, is a tough capsule built to survive fire, impact and sinking, so the record can be recovered after an accident. It retains data for up to 12 hours, keeping the most recent and recording over the oldest. The Data Acquisition Unit, or DAU, is the main unit that collects all the inputs, and it may have data storage for as long as 30 days. On the exam, both statements are true: up to 12 hours in the CSM, as long as 30 days in the DAU.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: Computers: follow the path. BIOS: P.O.S.T., bootstrap loader, BIOS drivers, BIOS setup
Ethernet: home runs to a central hub; CAT-5 with 4 twisted pairs
NMEA 0183: serial, RS422, single talker, ±15 V
NMEA 2000: 9-16 V, 1 LEN = 50 mA, 6 m drops, gateway
Depth 200-400 kHz; AIS 87B and 88B; rudder feedback; VDR: no EGC or MSI

onScreen: Computers: follow the path; BIOS: 4 functions
Instruments: depth, AIS, auto pilot, VDR
scenes.narration: Let's pull it together. Troubleshoot a computer by following the path, and remember the BIOS's 4 functions: P.O.S.T., the bootstrap loader, BIOS drivers and BIOS setup, where you check a computer that won't boot. Ethernet is a star of home run cables to a central hub, on CAT-5 with 4 twisted pairs. NMEA 0183 is serial, RS422, single talker, and survives plus or minus 15 volts. NMEA 2000 is a multi-talker CAN bus: 9 to 16 volts, 1 LEN is 50 milliamps, 6 meter drops, and a gateway to view it. On the bridge, depth finders use 200 to 400 kilohertz, AIS uses 87B and 88B, auto pilots need rudder feedback, and the VDR records neither EGC data nor MSI.
